source_text: τὰς θύρας τῆς σκηνῆς μὴ ἐνέγκῃ, ἐξολοθρευθήσεται ἡ ψυχὴ ἐκείνη ἐκ τοῦ λαοῦ αὐτῆς.» Ὅτι δὲ ἦν πᾶσά πως ἀνάγκη κατ' ἐκεῖνο καιροῦ τοὺς θύειν ἐθέλοντας, εἴς γε τὸν νεὼν καὶ εἰς τὴν ἁγίαν αὐτὴν ἀφικνεῖσθαι πόλιν, καὶ ἀποπεραίνειν ἐννόμως τὰ ἱερὰ, προσκομιζόντων αὐτὰ τῶν ἐξ αἵματος τοῦ Λευὶ, παρά σοι σαφῶς ἐπαΐειν Θεοῦ λέγοντος ἐναργῶς ἐν τῳ Δευτερονομίῳ· «Οὐ δυνήσῃ φαγεῖν ἐν ταῖς πόλεσί σου τὸ ἐπιδέκατον τοῦ σίτου σου, καὶ τοῦ οἴνου σου, καὶ τοῦ ἐλαίου σου, τὰ πρωτότοκα τῶν βοῶν σου, καὶ τῶν προβάτων σου, καὶ πάσας τὰς εὐχὰς, ὅσας ἂν εὔξῃ, καὶ τὰς ὁμολογίας ὑμῶν, καὶ τὰς ἀπαρχὰς τῶν χειρῶν ὑμῶν, ἀλλ' ἢ ἐναντίον Κυρίου τοῦ Θεοῦ σου φάγῃ αὐτὸ ἐν τῷ τόπῳ ᾧ ἂν ἐκλέξηται Κύριος ὁ Θεός σου αὑτῷ, σὺ καὶ οἱ υἱοί σου, καὶ ἡ θυγάτηρ σου, καὶ ὁ παῖς σου, καὶ ἡ παιδίσκη σου, καὶ ὁ Λευίτης, καὶ ὁ προσήλυτος ὁ ἐν ταῖς πόλεσί σου, καὶ εὐφρανθήσῃ ἐναντίον Κυρίου τοῦ Θεοῦ σου ἐπὶ πάντα, οὗ ἐὰν ἐπιβάλῃς τὴν χεῖρά σου· πρόσεχε σεαυτῷ μὴ ἐγκαταλίπῃς τὸν Λευίτην πάντα τὸν χρόνον ὅσον ἂν ζῇ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς.» Ἀπρόσιτον γὰρ τὸ Θεῖον, καὶ ἀπαράδεκτος ἡ θυσία Λευίτου δίχα· μεσιτεύουσι γὰρ, τὸν Θεοῦ καὶ ἀνθρώπων μεσίτην ἀπομιμούμενοι, τοῦτ' ἔστι Χριστόν. Ὅτι δὲ μία τέ ἐστιν ἡ Ἐκκλησία, καὶ ἓν τὸ Χριστοῦ μυστήριον, οὐκ ἔννομος δὲ θυσία, μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ ἀπόβλητος, καὶ τὸ ἁνδάνειν οὐκ ἔχουσα τῷ Θεῷ μὴ ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ τελουμένη, παρέδειξεν ἐναργῶς ὁ νόμος, μὴ δεῖν ἔξω λέγω τῆς ἁγίας σκηνῆς τελεῖσθαι τὰ ἱερά. Ὅση δὲ τῶν τοιούτων ἡ ἐπιτήρησις, εἴσῃ τοι κἀντεῦθεν. Ἦν μὲν γὰρ ἀπεικὸς οὐδὲν, μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ ἀληθὲς, μακροῖς διαστήμασι τοῖς διὰ μέσου κειμένοις ἀπονοσφίζεσθαι τῶν Ἱεροσολύμων τὰς ἀνὰ τὴν Ἰουδαίαν πᾶσαν οὐκ εὐαριθμήτους πόλεις. Καὶ τί τὸ ἐντεῦθεν σκληρὸν καὶ δυσήνυτον, τοὺς θύειν ἐθέλοντας ἀπαρχὴν σίτου, καὶ μὴν ἐλαίου καὶ οἴνου, τοσαύτην δύνασθαι διακομίσαι τὴν τρίβον; Ὄκνον δ' ἂν ἴσως ἐνεποίησέ τισιν, ὁ ὑπὸ χεῖρα πόνος, ἀλλ' ἦν ἀκαλλὲς, μᾶλλον δὲ τῶν ἄγαν ἐκτοπωτάτων, ἐπεί τοι τὸ χρῆμα δυσχερὲς, καὶ οὐκ εὐκατόρθωτον τοῖς ἀπωτέρω κειμένοις ἦν, παραλύεσθαι τῆς ἀληθείας τὸ κάλλος, οὐκ ἐν τῇ ἁγίᾳ σκηνῇ προσκομιζόντων τὰ ἱερὰ τῶν ἐξ Ἰσραήλ. Ἵνα τοίνυν ἁπάντων ἡμῖν τῶν ἐν μέσῳ παραποδισμάτων χρησίμως ἐξῃρημένων, καὶ εἰς τὸ τῷ νομοθέτῃ δοκοῦν διεξάγοιτο λοιπὸν ὁ ἐπὶ τῷδε νόμος, πεπαιδαγώγηκεν ὁ Μωσῆς, καὶ τὴν θείαν διερμηνεύει βούλησιν ἐν τῷ Δευτερονομίῳ, λέγων· «Δεκάτην ἀποδεκατώσεις παντὸς γεννήματος τοῦ σπέρματός σου, τὸ γέννημα τοῦ ἀγροῦ σου ἐνιαυτὸν κατ' ἐνιαυτὸν, καὶ φάγῃ αὐτὸ ἐναντίον Κυρίου τοῦ Θεοῦ σου ἐν τῷ τόπῳ ᾧ ἐὰν ἐκλέξηται Κύριος ὁ Θεός σου, ἐπικληθῆναι τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ, ἐκεῖ οἴσεις τὰ ἐπιδέκατα τοῦ σίτου σου, καὶ τοῦ οἴνου σου, καὶ τοῦ ἐλαίου σου, καὶ τὰ πρωτότοκα τῶν βοῶν σου, καὶ τῶν προβάτων σου, ἵνα μάθῃς φοβεῖσθαι Κύριον τὸν Θεόν σου πάσας τὰς ἡμέρας. Ἐὰν δὲ μακρὰν γένηται ἡ ὁδὸς ἀπὸ σοῦ, καὶ μὴ δύνῃ ἀναφέρειν αὐτὰ,

Nothing unlikely, rather true, that the not easily counted cities through all Judea were separated from Jerusalem by long intervals lying between. And what the hard and hard to accomplish thing from this: those wishing to sacrifice first fruit of grain, oil and wine to be able to convey so great a road. The labor at hand perhaps would have produced reluctance in some; but it was unseemly, rather among the most out of place, since the matter was difficult and not easily achieved for those lying farther off, for the beauty of the truth to be undone, those of Israel not bringing the sacred things in the holy tent. || So that all the obstacles in between being usefully removed for us, and the law on this might be carried through to what seems good to the lawgiver, Moses has instructed and interprets the divine will in Deuteronomy, saying: [Deut 14:22–24a LXX: a tenth you will tithe of all produce of your seed, the produce of your field year by year, and eat it before the Lord your God in the place he chooses for his name to be called on; there you will bring the tithes of grain, wine, oil, firstborn of oxen and sheep, that you may learn to fear the Lord your God all the days; but if the road becomes long from you and you are not able to carry them up…]
pass_b_english: Cyril: …does not bring it to the doors of the tent, that soul shall be utterly destroyed from among its people.’ (Leviticus 17:3–4) At that time those who wished to sacrifice were under every necessity to come to the temple and to the holy city itself, and to complete the sacred rites lawfully, with those of the blood of Levi presenting the offerings. You can hear this plainly from God, who says clearly in Deuteronomy: ‘You may not eat in your cities the tithe of your grain, of your wine and of your oil, the firstborn of your cattle and of your sheep, nor any of the vows that you vow, nor your freewill offerings, nor the first fruits of your hands; but you shall eat it only before the Lord your God, in the place which the Lord your God chooses for himself, you and your sons, and your daughter, and your male servant and your female servant, and the Levite and the stranger who is in your cities; and you shall rejoice before the Lord your God in everything to which you put your hand. Take care that you do not forsake the Levite for as long as he lives on the earth.’ (Deuteronomy 12:17–19) For the Divine is unapproachable, and a sacrifice without a Levite is unacceptable, since the Levites act as mediators, imitating the Mediator between God and humans, that is, Christ (1 Timothy 2:5). And the law showed plainly that the Church is one and the mystery of Christ is one, and that a sacrifice not performed in the Church is unlawful, or rather is to be rejected and cannot please God; I mean that it showed this by laying down that the sacred rites must not be performed outside the holy tent. You will learn from this too how much care was taken over such matters. It was not at all unlikely, indeed it was the case, that the cities throughout the whole of Judea, which were not easily counted, were separated from Jerusalem by the great distances lying between. And what hardship and toil followed from this? That those who wished to offer first fruits of grain, and of oil and wine as well, had to be able to carry them over so long a road. The labor involved might perhaps have made some reluctant. Yet it was unseemly, indeed utterly out of place, that because the thing was hard and not easy to accomplish for those who lived farther away, the beauty of the truth should be impaired, with the Israelites not bringing their offerings to the holy tent. So, in order that every obstacle in the way might be usefully removed for us, and that the law on this matter might from then on be carried out as the lawgiver intended, Moses gives instruction and sets out the divine will in Deuteronomy, saying: ‘You shall set apart a tenth of all the produce of your seed, the produce of your field, year by year, and you shall eat it before the Lord your God in the place which the Lord your God chooses for his name to be called upon. There you shall bring the tithes of your grain, of your wine and of your oil, and the firstborn of your cattle and of your sheep, so that you may learn to fear the Lord your God at all times. But if the road is too long for you, and you are not able to carry them up… (Deuteronomy 14:22–24)

choices.why: Deut 12:17–19: ὁμολογίαι rendered 'freewill offerings' (the LXX term for Hebrew nedabot in this verse).

anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of De adoratione Book 13 to compare. Sense taken from the PG 68 Greek. The withheld earlier English was not used as a model.

apparatus.note: Section opens mid-quotation (Leviticus 17:3–4 LXX, begun at the end of section 18 with ἐὰν δέ τις θύσῃ… καὶ ἐπὶ) and mid-turn; 'Cyril: …' follows the Book 13 convention for continued turns, and the quotation mark opened in section 18 closes after 'its people'. The wording matches Lev 17:3–4 (calf/sheep slain in the camp, not brought to the door of the tent, that soul destroyed from its people); Lev 17:8–9 has the same penalty clause but concerns burnt offerings by anyone of Israel or the proselytes, so 17:3–4 is preferred. Deut 12:17–19: ὁμολογίαι rendered 'freewill offerings' (the LXX term for Hebrew nedabot in this verse). The source reads ζῇ ('he lives'); the LXX reads ζῇς ('you live'); I follow the printed text ('all the time that he lives on the earth') and flag it as a probable slip for ζῇς. The 'Mediator between God and humans' (μεσίτης Θεοῦ καὶ ἀνθρώπων) is a clear echo of 1 Timothy 2:5 and is cited. ἐκκλησίᾳ in 'not performed in the Church' is lower-case in Migne but carries the same sense as the preceding Ἐκκλησία; rendered 'the Church' both times. 'And what hard and toilsome thing followed from this?' keeps Cyril's question form (καὶ τί τὸ ἐντεῦθεν σκληρὸν καὶ δυσήνυτον). Section ends mid-quotation inside Deuteronomy 14:24 (…μὴ δύνῃ ἀναφέρειν αὐτά); the sentence continues in section 20, so the paragraph ends on a comma with the quotation still open. In 14:23 the printed punctuation joins ἐκεῖ to οἴσεις ('There you shall bring'); followed. Review: the 14:23 rendering previously had 'called upon there' and also 'There you shall bring', translating ἐκεῖ twice; the doubled 'there' is removed.

review.method: translate from the Greek, then a separate clause-by-clause review against the Greek
changes: Removed 'himself' after 'God' (not in Greek); split the fronted ὅτι-clause into two sentences in natural order
Deut 12:19: 'Take heed to yourself… all the time that' -> 'Take care… for as long as' (archaism and calque)
ἀπαράδεκτος: 'is not accepted' -> 'is unacceptable'; kept γάρ as 'since'
Reordered 'How much care… you will learn' to natural order
ἦν ἀπεικὸς οὐδέν: 'not at all unlikely'; 'lay cut off… in between' -> 'were separated… by the great distances lying between'
Deut 14:22: 'tithe a tenth' -> 'set apart a tenth'; 14:23 doubled 'there' removed; 'all the days' -> 'at all times'
Tense: 'Moses gave instruction and explains' -> 'Moses gives instruction and sets out'
assembly_edits: book-wide consistency: outer quotation marks ‘ ’, lower-case pronouns for God, US spelling, σκηνή = 'tent'
reader-facing translator_notes: row-join and review-history sentences removed; full note kept in apparatus
